title: Supernova bubbles may keep Andromeda's gas in motion
freshness: Published in Nature Astronomy on 17 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Using China's FAST radio telescope and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, a Tsinghua-led team mapped 118 expanding superbubbles in Andromeda. The energy those bubbles deliver lines up with the energy needed to keep the galaxy's neutral hydrogen turbulent, in magnitude and across the disk.
whyItMatters: Turbulence in galactic gas keeps losing energy, and something has to supply it or star-forming clouds would settle. Andromeda now has a counted population of superbubbles whose input matches that loss, in size and in how both change with distance from the center. Clustered supernovae are the driver the team names.

body:
## A problem posed in 1979

In 1979, Carl Heiles found giant shells of neutral hydrogen in the Milky Way. Neutral hydrogen, often called HI, is cold atomic hydrogen gas, the kind radio telescopes map. Some of those shells span hundreds or thousands of light-years. The largest one required more energy than a single supernova could supply. Structures like that are called superbubbles. A superbubble is a giant cavity blown when stellar winds and repeated supernova explosions from a group of massive stars sweep the surrounding gas into a shell.

The same objects brush against a second, older question. What keeps turbulence going? Turbulence here means irregular gas motions on many scales, the kind that help decide how fast clouds collapse into stars. Those motions continuously lose energy. The fraction of supernova energy that actually reaches the gas has been hard to pin down, so it has been easy to assume an efficiency and hard to measure one. A team led by Professor Di Li at Tsinghua University used superbubbles in the Andromeda galaxy to replace that assumption with a number taken from the gas itself.

## 118 shells, weighed from the gas

Andromeda, also called M31, lies about 2.5 million light-years away. That distance is a gift. We see the whole disk from outside, which is a view we cannot have of the Milky Way from the inside. The team combined China's FAST radio telescope with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in the United States. FAST is sensitive to the diffuse gas. The VLA picks up the fine structure of the shells. Together they show both.

The map contains 118 expanding superbubbles. Some expand slowly, with estimated ages up to 40 million years. An old, slow shell still counts. Turbulence has to be driven for a long time, not in a single blast, and a bubble that has been growing for tens of millions of years is a record of prolonged energy input.

The observations supplied three quantities for the shells: size, expansion speed, and the density of the gas around them. From those, the team estimated the kinetic energy transferred into the gas and how long the input lasted. Divide energy by time and you have an average rate. That rate is the replacement for an assumed transfer efficiency. It is estimated from the bubbles and their surroundings, not inserted by hand so that a model will balance.

The paper, "Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles," was published online in Nature Astronomy on 17 September 2026. Di Li's group in Tsinghua's Department of Astronomy led the work, with the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and international collaborators. Tsinghua is the first-listed affiliation. Fanyi Meng of Tsinghua and Chao-Wei Tsai and Jingwen Wu of the National Astronomical Observatories share first authorship. Di Li is the corresponding author.

## The rates agree, in size and across the disk

The team also estimated how quickly the turbulence loses energy, taking galactic rotation and thermal motions into account. The input rate from the superbubbles and the loss rate of the turbulence agree in magnitude. They also agree in how they vary with distance from the galaxy's center. A match that is only a single galaxy-wide total could be a coincidence of averages. A match that follows the same trend from the inner disk to the outer disk is harder to wave off.

This is the sense in which the energy in the bubbles closely matches the energy needed to sustain the galaxy's turbulence. Tsinghua compares rates, injection against dissipation, and the agreement is in magnitude and in the trend with radius. No percentage is stated, and none is added here. Their figure marks injection rates, a band for turbulent losses, an estimated contribution from the magnetorotational instability (rotation plus magnetic fields), and an earlier bubble sample. Another driver is on the plot. The text's claim is that clustered supernovae can maintain M31's neutral-hydrogen turbulence.

"Can maintain" is a sufficiency claim about the neutral hydrogen. It is not a claim that every other driver contributes zero, and the figure's extra shading is a reminder of that. It is also not a claim about every phase of the gas. The turbulence in question is the turbulence in the atomic hydrogen. Molecular clouds and hot halo gas are a different measurement.

## What was counted, and what the driver claim adds

Counted: 118 expanding superbubbles, their sizes, their speeds, the densities around them, and ages up to about 40 million years for the slow ones. Derived from those counts: kinetic energy, duration, and an average power delivered to the gas, plus a separate estimate of how fast turbulence drains. Inferred: successive supernovae, collected into superbubbles, supply enough energy to sustain the observed neutral-hydrogen turbulence in Andromeda. The paper's title is stronger than "contribute." It says the supernova origin is revealed. The evidence offered for that sentence is the rate comparison, including the shared trend with radius.

Heiles's largest shells already showed that one explosion underfills the biggest cavities. A group of massive stars pours wind into the same volume and then explodes over millions of years. The cavities merge into a superbubble. In Andromeda, 118 of them can be added up, and the motion they leave is a galactic energy budget rather than a local scar.

Later stars form from the gas those explosions stirred, so the budget reaches the next generation. Andromeda is one resolvable spiral, not a stand-in for every galaxy. The scope is this map and this galaxy's neutral hydrogen.

Tsinghua's note is the group's summary. Nature Astronomy is the authority for the fits and the other drivers. Groups of exploding stars have inflated 118 giant bubbles in Andromeda's atomic gas, and the power in those bubbles lines up with the power the turbulence requires.
